texts.preamble: State vs . Pratap Singh on 6 August, 2012 In The Court Of Sh. Sushil Anuj Tyagi, Metropolitan Magistrate: Rohini Courts, Delhi Fir No. 167/06 P.S. Kanjhawala State Vs. Pratap Singh Unique Id No. 02404Ro378182010 Date of Institution : 29.3.2008 Date of reserving of judgment : 31.7.2012 Date of judgment : 06.8.2012 J U D G M E N T
texts.facts: 8. Final Order : Acquitted 9. Date of final order : 06.8.2012 BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR THE DECISION: 1. Succinctly, the facts of the case as per prosecution are that on FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala 10.10.2006 at about 1:15pm at FCI Godown Unit No. 3, Ghevra Delhi accused Pratap Singh was working as contractor and he was negligent at the time of welding work and due to which one Shiv Narayan Shah fell down from the roof and later on died due to to the injuries received by him due to negligent act of accused, not amounting to culpable homicide. Matter was reported to police, accused was arrested and upon completion of further necessary investigation charge sheet was prepared and was filed in the court for trial. 2. The copies of chargesheet and annexed documents were supplied to accused persons in due compliance of Section 207 Cr.P.C. 3. Prima facie case having been made out, notice for the offence U/s 304A IPC was served upon the accused on 20.12.2008 to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 4. In order to prove its case prosecution examined following witnesses: State vs . Pratap Singh on 6 August, 2012 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21456150/ 1 5. PW 1 Dr. V.K. Jha proved the postmortem report of deceased Shiv Narayan Shah as Ex. PW 1/A and proved his signatures at point A upon the same. 6. PW 2 Ramesh Kumar deposed that on 10.10.2006 he was posted at Food Storage Depot Ghevra as Manager (civil) and work of welding was going on in godown No. 3 and one labour died due to fall from the roof when he was working . He further deposed that accused Pratap Singh was the Incharge of the work being the contractor. When he received the information that the labour died he immediately informed the police at No. 100 and being the contractor, all the FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala responsibilities of the work and mishap was of accused Pratap Singh. He further deposed that he cannot say whether this accident occurred due to the negligency of accused, as he was not the eye witness of the accident. He further submitted that during investigation he submitted the photocopy of office order No. 22/2004 which is Ex PW2/A and the work order Mark A to the IO. 7. PW 3 Hari Parkash deposed that it was the incident of the year 2006. On that day he was working as welder at FCI Godwn, Ghevra and deceased Shiv Narayan was his helper. He was doing welding work at ventilator and suddenly decesed fell down from the roof. He further deposed that he found that the fiber sheet of the roof was broken and he fell down from the roof. He further deposed that accused Pratap Singh was the incharge of the work being the contractor. He further deposed that there was no fault of accused Pratap. This witness was declared hostile and was cross examined by ld APP for the state. 8. PW 4 HC Rajender Prasad was posted as duty officer in PS Kanjhawala and registered the FIR in the present case. He proved the copy of FIR as Ex. PW 4/A and endorsement on rukka as Ex. PW 4/B. He further proved the DD No. 20A and 23A as Ex. PW 4/C and Ex. PW 4/D. 9. PW 5 Ct. Sunil deposed that on 10.10.2006 on receipt of PCR call he alongwith HC Balraj reached at FCI Godown A3, Ghevra and SI V.D. Pandey also reached there and they found a dead body there. During inquiry name of deceased was revealed as Shiv Narain. He further deposed that IO prepared FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala rukka and got registered the FIR through him . After that he took the dead body to SGM Hospital and got preserved the same and on the next day postmortem on the dead body was got conducted. 10. PW 6 SI V. D Pandey is the investigating officer of the case. He deposed that on 10.10.2006 on receipt of DD 20A already Ex PW4/C, he alongwith Ct. Sunil reached FCI godown no. A3 Ghevra where they found one dead body of Shiv Narayan and came to know that the deceased has fallen from the roof while doing welding. He got the spot photographed and prepared rukka Ex. PW6/A and got FIR registered through Ct. Sunil. After that he prepared site plan Ex PW6/B and sent the dead body to SGM Mortuary and got the postmortem conducted. PM report is already Ex PW1/A. He collected documents with regard to contract of work Ex PW6/C and work order Mark A. Thereafter accused was arrested vide memo Ex PW6/D and his personal search was conducted vide memo Ex PW6/E. Thereafter challan was prepared and filed in court. 11. Thereafter statement of accused was recorded U/s 313 Cr.PC on 30.3.2012 wherein he denied all the incriminating material available on record against him. He stated that he has been falsely State vs . Pratap Singh on 6 August, 2012 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21456150/ 2 implicated in this case. He further stated that that he was not present on the spot at the time of accident and the working of welding was given to Hari Prakash and the deceased was hired by Hari Prakash. He further stated that deceased was not working under his control. 12. I have carefully perused the case record and have heard arguments FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala advanced by ld APP for the state as well as by ld defence counsel. 13. The accused Pratap Singh in the present case is charged for the offence U/s 304A IPC on the facts that on 10.10.2006 at FCI Godown, he acted negligently due to which the deceased Shiv Narayan Shah fell down from rook and died.
texts.arguments: 14. Section 304A IPC reads as: Section 304A. Causing death by negligence 304A. Causing death by negligence.--Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. 15. It was FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala held by the Apex court in State Of Haryana vs Jagbir Singh And Anr decided on 26 September, 2003 in Appeal (crl.) 1721 of 1996 that: "In Hanumant Govind Nargundkar and Anr. V. State of Madhya Pradesh, (AIR 1952 SC 343), wherein it was observed thus: "It is well to remember that in cases where the evidence is of a circumstantial nature, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be in the first instance be fully established and all the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused. Again, the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency and they should be such as to exclude every hypothesis but the one proposed to be proved. In other words, there must be a chain of evidence so far complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and it must be such as to show that within all human probability the act must State vs . Pratap Singh on 6 August, 2012 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21456150/ 3 have been done by the accused." A reference may be made to a later decision in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, (AIR 1984 SC 1622). Therein, while dealing with circumstantial evidence, it has been held that onus was on the prosecution to prove that the chain is complete and the infirmity of lacuna in prosecution cannot be cured by false defence or plea. The conditions precedent in the words of this Court, before conviction could be based on circumstantial evidence, must be fully established. They are: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established. FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; (4) they should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved; and (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused." 18. In AIR 2001 SUPREME COURT 3660 "M. S. Grewal v. Deep Chand Sood", it as observed that: "14. Negligence in common parlance mean and imply 'failure to exercise due care, expected of a reasonable prudent person'. It is a breach of duty and negligence in law ranging from inadvertence to shameful disregard of safety of others. In most instances, it is caused by heedlessness or inadvertence, by with the negligent party is unaware of the results which may follow from his act. negligence is thus a breach of duty or lack of proper care in doing something, in short, it is want of attention and doing of something which a prudent and a reasonable man would not do (vide FIR No. 167/06 PS Kanjhawala Black's Law Dictionary). Though sometimes, the word 'inadvertence' stands and used as a synonym to negligence, but in effect negligence represents a state of the mind which however is much serious in nature than mere inadvertence. There is thus existing a differentiation between the two expressions whereas inadvertence is a milder form of negligence, 'negligence' by itself mean and imply a state of mind where there is no regard for duty or the supposed care and attention which one ought to bestow. Clerk and Lindsell on Torts (18th Ed.) sets out State vs . Pratap Singh on 6 August, 2012 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21456150/ 4 four several requirements of the tort of negligence and the same read as below : "(1) the existence in law of a duty of care situation, i.e. one in which the law attaches liability to carelessness. There has to be recognition by law that the careless infliction of the kind of damage in suit on the class of person to which the claimant belongs by the class of person to which the defendant belongs is actionable; (2) breach of the duty of care by the defendant, i.e. that it failed to measure up to the standard set by law; (3) a casual connection between the defendant's careless conduct and the damage; (4) that the particular kind of damage to the particular claimant is not so unforeseeable as to be too remote." 19. Also in 1969 CRI. L. J. 977 (V. 75, C. N. 269) "State v. Narhari", it was observed that: "3. ..... It may also be stated that an accused starts with a presumption of innocence in his favour, and that this presumption is reinforced by an acquittal judgment. This is a wellsettled principle. A remote nexus is not enough.
